wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.rappels: 1-2 fixed rappels on upper ridge; additional rappels may be necessary in poor conditions
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.beta: Grade IV alpine ice climbing with 40-60 degree steep snow and ice; 5,512 ft technical climbing from ridge base (8,600 ft) to Liberty Cap (14,112 ft); 5.7 pitches; requires Alpine Ice Grade III+ experience and multi-day expedition commitment; crux is sustained steep ice and exposed ridge sections with high rockfall hazard from Willis Wall above Carbon Glacier

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.approach: Two approaches are used, both arduous. The Paradise approach (5,420 ft) follows the Skyline Trail to the Nisqually Moraine Trail, then a climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, where several boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier itself; most parties rope up here, since the crossing threads through heavily crevassed terrain exposed to icefall from above and is genuinely dangerous in reduced visibility. From the glacier's east moraine there are two ways up onto Wapowety Cleaver: a flat traverse to the base of 'The Fan,' a gully with avalanche, rockfall, and steep-slope hazard, climbed directly to a bench at 7,300 ft; or a climb up the Nisqually/Wilson Glacier margin at 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft 'Wilson Bench.' From the bench, snow slopes lead to the ridge crest and a string of established camps at increasing elevation — Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft), and the Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft, the most common base for a summit push, with running water from mid-June on). The alternative Van Trump Park approach starts at the Comet Falls Trailhead (3,650 ft): follow the maintained Comet Falls Trail 2.2 miles (2,000 ft gain) to a junction, continue toward Van Trump Park another 0.6 miles to where maintained trail ends, then follow unmaintained social trails up a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, followed up to the Upper Castle (9,500 ft) where the two approaches merge — descending this line requires a saved GPS track to relocate the correct moraine and treeline trail junction, even in good visibility, per NPS guidance. Above the Castle, established high camps continue at Camp Hazard (10,800 ft, at the base of the Turtle Snowfield — stick to the west/climber's-right-avoiding side, since the snowfield's center and east are raked by ice and rockfall off the Kautz Ice Cliff), the Rock Step camps (11,250 ft), and exposed Wapowety Cleaver bivy sites (13,100 ft, used mainly by parties planning to descend via the Disappointment Cleaver rather than reverse the Kautz).

wa_mount_rainier_fuhrer_finger.overview: A prominent snow/ice couloir ('finger') splitting the cliffs between the Nisqually and Wilson Glaciers, giving one of the more direct lines up Rainier's south side. From Camp Muir the route crosses the Nisqually Glacier and Wilson Glacier, then climbs a narrowing gully at 35-45° that leads onto the upper Nisqually Glacier; the Finger itself pinches to a few hundred feet wide at roughly 40-50°. Above the Finger the route continues up along the Wilson Cleaver — with a short section around 60° — to about 13,500 ft, where the angle eases toward the summit.
wa_mount_rainier_fuhrer_finger.approach: From Paradise (5,400 ft), follow the Skyline Trail past Panorama Point and Pebble Creek onto the Muir Snowfield to Camp Muir (10,080 ft), roughly 4.5 miles and ~4,600 ft of gain. From Camp Muir, descend and traverse west across the Nisqually Glacier to the Wilson Glacier and the base of the Fuhrer Finger.

wa_mount_rainier_edmunds_headwall.approach: From Mowich Lake, traverse to the Edmunds/South Mowich glaciers and the base of the headwall.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.overview: Frostbite Ridge is the classic alpine route on Glacier Peak — a long, aesthetic ridge on the north/northwest side that links snow, ice, and a short mixed crux past the 'Rabbit Ears' gendarmes. Combined with the peak's deep remoteness, it's a committing grade III–IV outing and one of the great moderate alpine traverses in the North Cascades.

wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face.overview: A steep snow-and-ice face on the northeast side of Forbidden Peak. Best in firm early-season conditions, it offers sustained steep ice climbing in a shaded, remote North Cascades cirque.
wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face.rappels: Same as East Ledges: ~5 single-rope rappels, approximately 400 ft total

wa_mount_index_north_face.rappels: Descend by rappelling the route on existing fixed and natural anchors; multiple double-rope rappels are needed, some on rockfall-damaged bolts, so carry extra webbing/cord.
wa_mount_index_north_face.beta: From the talus/grass slopes on the rockslide on the west side of Lake Serene, the route gains a wooded ridge above the lake and ascends the north rib for three leads (the first two on solid, exposed class-5.5 rock) to an open, grassy bench, then continues via further pitches and scrambling to the North Peak's summit ridge and top. The face has several documented variations; a separately catalogued 'Direct Northeast Face' line on the same wall is rated 5.6 over 8-12 pitches, and may overlap with or vary from this description.

wa_the_brothers_traverse.descent_text: Reverse the ridge traverse carefully, managing rope carefully on exposed sections. Once south of the saddle, descend the east-facing gully to the 5,500 ft base camp area, then retrace the trail descent to Lena Lake Trailhead (additional 4-5 hours).

wa_cutthroat_peak_cauthorn_wilson_couloi.beta: Grade II, 5.7 climbing. Short approach from highway. Rock improves significantly higher on ridge. Fair granite in approach, improves on ridge. Moderate exposure. Quick alpine climb from Rainy Pass. Uncrowded route.

wa_cutthroat_west_ridge.beta: Grade II, 5.7 climbing. Short approach from highway. Rock improves significantly higher on ridge. Fair granite in approach, improves on ridge. Moderate exposure. Quick alpine climb from Rainy Pass. Uncrowded route.

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.beta: From a high camp below the Boulder Glacier (~5,500 ft), follow the Boulder-Park Cleaver northwest onto the lower Boulder Glacier. Above about 9,300 ft, choose between a moderate 25-35° snow traverse toward Sherman Crater, or a harder 4th-class rock buttress direct to the summit area.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.approach: From Sedro-Woolley, drive SR 20 east 16 miles to milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Highway (FR 11) for about 18 miles, then (after Boulder Creek Campground) turn onto FR 1130 for about 1 mile to FR 1131, and follow it to the Boulder Ridge Trailhead. Hike the Boulder Ridge Trail (maintained about 2 miles to the wilderness boundary), then a steep, unmaintained boot path with a 3rd-class rock band around 3.4 mi/4,700 ft, continuing along a lateral moraine to the Boulder/Park Glacier near 6,300 ft and a high camp around 5,500 ft.

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.approach: From I-90 Exit 85, take Highway 970 east 7 miles to Teanaway Road, then bear right onto North Fork Teanaway Road continuing 22.5 miles total. From trailhead: northeast via Lake Ingalls to Goat Pass (east-northeast), then south to Stuart Glacier and North Ridge notch
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.fa: Great Gendarme: John Rupley & Don Gordon, 1956; complete upper-ridge linkup (from the Stuart Glacier notch): James Wickwire & Fred Stanley, 1964

wa_the_direct_north_ridge_w_gendarme.fa: North Ridge (original line, bypassing the Great Gendarme): Don Claunch & John Rupley, September 9, 1956. First ascent climbing directly over the Great Gendarme: Fred Beckey & Steve Marts, 1963. Direct lower-ridge start variation (from the true toe): Mead Hargis & Jay Ossiander, 1970

wa_mount_stuart_west_ridge.approach: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (end of North Fork Teanaway Road, ~4,243 ft) and follow the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.4 mile, stay right/straight at the Longs Pass junction rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin, and switchback up open slopes to Longs Pass (5 mi, ~2,100 ft gain from the trailhead, cresting around 6,400 ft) — the pass gives the first clear look at Stuart's west aspect. From the pass, descend steep, sometimes dusty/scree-y trail on the north side, losing close to 1,000 ft, to reach Ingalls Creek in the timber below. Cross the creek (a straightforward rock-hop or wade in normal summer flow, the last reliable water source before the ridge) and pick up the climber's path heading east/upvalley toward Stuart Pass. Well short of the pass itself (roughly 6,200–6,400 ft), leave the trail and traverse climber's-left (north) across open talus and heather benches toward the base of the West Ridge — this cross-country traverse is where parties most commonly go astray, since there is no maintained tread and several minor gullies look similar; aim for the obvious deep gully (the middle of three parallel gullies) marked by a large, house-sized boulder at its base. An alternate, longer northern approach via the Stuart Lake Trailhead and Stuart Pass exists but adds significant mileage and is not the standard line. Plan on 3.5–5 hours car-to-base depending on route-finding and snow conditions; some parties camp near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin to break the day up. Hazards: the Longs Pass descent and creek-crossing slopes hold snow into early summer and can be icy at dawn; the final talus traverse to the ridge is loose and exposed to rockfall from parties above; there is no water beyond the Ingalls Creek crossing, so tank up there for the long day ahead. The route works past Long John Tower via either a short dihedral with a fixed piton (5.4) or a layback further along the ledge (5.6) before regaining the ridge crest; this and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse are the route's main route-finding dilemmas.

wa_vanishing_point.beta: Vanishing Point is approximately as steep a route as one could find on the mountain—nearly every pitch involves relentless overhanging terrain at 5.11–5.12. The route was established over several years and fully modernized in 2020 with new stainless-steel anchors and improved protection. Notable features include pitch 5 (crux, 5.12+), a collapsed roof section, and several intentionally runout pitches. The approach involves 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab climbing with fixed lines and bolts. Published pitch counts vary between 14 and 20 depending on how the climbing is split or linked; the pitch-by-pitch breakdown here uses the 20-pitch convention.
wa_vanishing_point.rappels: Rappel anchors have been updated to stainless steel and are spaced roughly 30-35 m apart on the tower and along the fixed-line sections of the approach; the approach can be reversed with a single 70 m rope where the updated anchors allow it. Most parties do not rappel the route — they top out and walk off via the BASE-jumper trail.

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.overview: Snoqualmie Mountain is the highest summit rising directly above the Alpental ski area at Snoqualmie Pass, one of the most-climbed scrambles near Seattle for its short approach and big views of Chair Peak, The Tooth, and Guye Peak across the valley. The peak actually has two summits about 550 ft apart: the popular west summit reached by this standard climbers' path, and a slightly higher east summit (about 3 ft taller per a 2023 professional GPS survey) that requires down-climbing into a notch and an exposed 4th-class move across a gap — most parties doing the standard route skip it.

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.beta: From Hannegan Pass, parties gain Ruth Mountain (via its glacier/snow slopes), then descend Ruth's south ridge — 'talus and slabs below a rock ridge' with casual 2nd-3rd class climbing on generally good rock — to the Ruth-Icy Saddle, from which Icy Peak is clearly visible. From the saddle, crampon up firm snow toward the notch between Icy's Northwest and Southeast summits, then climb the Southeast Peak's Northwest Ridge — reported as 'steep, loose, wildly exposed' — to a Class 4 knife-edge summit ridge leading to the true (Southeast) summit, finishing with a 100-ft 4th-class summit gully.

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.overview: North Twin Sister (6,644 ft) is the second-highest and northernmost summit of the Twin Sisters Range, a massif of dunite (mantle-derived, olivine-rich rock) about 10 miles southwest of Mount Baker. This line approaches from the south/southwest and gains the ridge connecting North and South Twin before finishing up solid, high-friction olivine to the north summit - the same rock quality that makes the West Ridge famous, reached via a different line up the mountain.

wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.beta: Where the standard Gerdine Ridge/Cool Glacier route would traverse onto the Suiattle Glacier around 8,000-8,500 ft, this variant instead continues directly up the nose of the cleaver on a climber's trail (when melted out), steepening into mostly 3rd/4th class terrain (with a few 5th-class moves) between about 8,500 ft and Disappointment Peak's 9,755 ft summit. From there, descend slightly to the saddle above the Cool Glacier to rejoin the standard route to Glacier Peak's summit. The main appeal is avoiding glacier travel and crevasse hazard entirely, traded for sustained loose, rockfall-prone scrambling.

wa_cashmere_mountain_se_route.beta: From the Eightmile Trail, cut cross-country up through an old burn zone, then continue up and left toward the gully between the S and SE ridges. The S/SE gully is wide and offers a 'choose your own adventure' character: the center/right line is mostly class 2, while the climbers-left side holds solid class 3-4 rock. The gully steepens into its class-3 crux above roughly 8,150 ft, about 360 vertical feet below the 8,514 ft summit. This line cuts the standard 8-9 mile one-way West Ridge approach roughly in half.
